picked.t: American fine-dining steakhouse to open first Asia restaurant in Ho Chi Minh City
picked.body: The restaurant will be located in the Bitexco Financial Tower in the heart of Ho Chi Minh City, giving the brand a prominent presence in one of Southeast Asia's fastest-growing markets, Darden Restaurants that owns the chain said in a press release. To span approximately 500 square meters, the restaurant will accomodate 120 seats, a bar, three private dining rooms, a temperature- and humidity-controlled dry aging room, a butcher room and a wine cellar. The restaurant is renowned for steaks that are dry-aged in-house for 18 to 24 days before being hand-carved by an on-site butcher. Ho Chi Minh City has seen a vibrant dining landscape joined by various international restaurant and hospitality brands. The city is home to five one-Michelin-starred restaurants: Anan Saigon, Akuna, Long Trieu, CieL, and Coco Dining.

picked.t: Ha Giang man goes from motorbike driver to tourism entrepreneur
picked.body: In early 2023, Thuat, then 32, a native of Ha Giang (now part of Tuyen Quang Province), quit his job at a company in the Bac Ninh Industrial Park, where he was earning more than VND20 million (US$800) a month. Living far from home, facing work pressure, and feeling that the job was not a good fit, he decided to return home and look for work that would allow him to stay close to his family while offering long-term growth opportunities based on his hometown’s tourism potential. Three days after quitting, he went to Hanoi to buy a camera, spent a week studying tourist attractions and visitors’ needs, and picking the brains of some people experienced in tourism. He then began by taking tourists by motorbike to destinations such as Tham Ma Slope, Ma Pi Leng Pass, and Lo Lo Chai and shooting photos of them for free. All he asked was for them to post the photos and recommend his services to others. For the first few months, he only had three or four customers a week, and none at all sometimes. On days when he had customers, he earned VND300,000-500,000. "The hardest part was that customers did not know who I was or whether they could trust me since most of them came from southern provinces," he says. Local tourism is seasonal, with visitor numbers rising during flower and rice-harvest seasons but falling sharply during periods of heavy rain and storms. To better understand the needs of visitors, he spent time studying travel routes, checking service quality so he could offer tourists informed advice, and listening to their feedback. Finding customers through social media was also difficult because many groups required users to pay for advertising posts. Noticing that room-booking scams and misleading advertisements were becoming increasingly common as visitor numbers increased but tourists lacked a reliable source of comprehensive information, he launched the "Ha Giang Review Tat Tan Tat" (Review everything about Ha Giang) community in October 2023. The group allows members to share information about destinations and services, and accommodation providers and restaurants to promote themselves for free. To prevent misinformation, Thuat often visits businesses in person to verify information before approving posts. The community got one million members within seven months, surpassed two million in two years, and now has around 2.3 million members, a figure many KOLs long for. According to Ly Thai Chu, deputy chief of the Office of the People's Council and People's Committee of Ha Giang 2 Ward, Thuat has good understanding of tourism, is enthusiastic, and has come up with many initiatives to support local tourism. Thuat's community has grown rapidly thanks to its free, up-to-date information and its role in connecting tourists with service providers. However, its large scale also creates a need for tighter control over the accuracy of advertisements as the admin team still occasionally allows inaccurate information to slip through. Thuat said the group receives hundreds of posts and thousands of comments every day. The biggest challenge is balancing members' right to report problems with the responsibility to protect the reputations of the service providers involved. When inaccurate information is discovered, he tries to verify it quickly, issue an apology and a correction or remove the post. Ha Van Minh, a tourist from Hanoi, said the group had occasionally approved inaccurate content, such as incorrect information about when photos were taken, but "the admins are quick to correct mistakes, and so this is a tourism community I trust for information." Thuat now has seven staff members who help manage the group in shifts. After each incident, the team reviews its procedures and requires people submitting posts to provide clearer evidence. Three years after returning home, Thuat had progressed from being a motorbike taxi driver taking tourists around to managing service procurement and sales at a local travel company. At the end of 2025, he set up a company specializing in tours and transportation services for both international and domestic visitors in Tuyen Quang. The community has also raised his profile, helping increase service bookings by 50-60%. He now gets an average of 60-70 customers a day, with bookings rising by five to six times during the Lunar New Year and other holidays. Yet, whenever he has free time, he still takes his camera to tourist attractions across Tuyen Quang to photograph visitors for free just as he did three years ago. Thuat's current income is 1.5 to two times what he earned while working in Bac Ninh. What means the most to him, however, are the messages of thanks from tourists he has advised and protected from scammers. Chu Thuy Linh of Hanoi once nearly lost almost VND10 million after booking a non-existent hotel. picked.t: These are the best fine dining restaurants in Vietnam
picked.body: The Rhythms , located on the seventh floor of Hanoi's La Sinfonía del Rey Hotel & Spa, tops the list. The restaurant serves refined cuisine alongside cocktails and premium wines and features an outdoor dining area overlooking Hoan Kiem Lake and Hanoi's Old Quarter. Its west-facing terrace offers views of the sunset, making it a popular spot for diners looking to enjoy the cityscape with friends or loved ones. In addition to popular international dishes, its menu showcases authentic Vietnamese cuisine, featuring regional specialties from across the country such as chicken roasted in northwest Vietnam style and spring rolls. Address: 33 - 35 Hang Dau Street, Hoan Kiem Ward, Hanoi Reflections , located on the third floor of the Caravelle Saigon Hotel, ranks second. The restaurant overlooks the Saigon Opera House and offers an upscale setting with a three-course menu centered on international fine dining. Tripadvisor highlighted its Wagyu beef steak and chef's degustation menu, while praising the friendly and professional services. Address: ​​​​19 Lam Son Square, Saigon Ward, HCMC Khue Restaurant , located on the 12th floor of Le Jardin Hotel Haute Couture, is third on the list. Tripadvisor described the restaurant as a special-occasion dining destination, highlighting its elegant decor and carefully crafted menu. Address: 105 Nguyen Truong To Street, Ba Dinh Ward, Hanoi. Olivine Restaurant , located on the rooftop of Peridot Grand Luxury Boutique Hotel in Hanoi, is fourth on the list. "The staff’s friendly style and attention to detail make things feel special without being over the top. Go for anything the chef recommends—especially if there’s a seasonal tasting menu," Tripadvisor wrote, recommending the restaurant for its fusion of Western culinary techniques. Address: 33 Duong Thanh Street, Hoan Kiem Ward, Hanoi Mizumi Westlake – Sushi, Teppanyaki & Omakase ranks fifth. The Japanese restaurant offers three dining styles: omakase, teppanyaki and à la carte. Its menu features a wide selection of Japanese dishes, while the rooftop Sky Lounge offers views of West Lake. Advance reservations are recommended. Address: 51 Xuan Dieu Street, Tay Ho Ward, Hanoi. French Grill Restaurant in the lobby of the five-star JW Marriott Hotel Hanoi ranks sixth. The restaurant offers classic French cuisine with a local twist and has gained popularity among foreign visitors. Its menu features dishes such as seared foie gras, classic caviar, and premium steaks, with prices ranging from VND300,000 to VND700,000 (US$11.55-27). The restaurant operates daily from 6 p.m. to 10:30 p.m. Address: 8 Do Duc Duc Street, Nam Tu Liem Ward, Hanoi Towa - Japanese Cuisine , on the 28th floor of Sedona Suites near Ben Thanh Market, ranks seventh. Thanks to its convenient location and ideal vantage point for fireworks, the restaurant is often crowded during the New Year and Lunar New Year holidays. Its signature dishes include rock shrimp tempura, Anago tempura and grilled Wagyu beef with truffle cream sauce. Address: 94 Nam Ky Khoi Nghia, Saigon Ward, HCMC Lai Restaurant , also o n the 28th floor of Sedona Suites, ranks eighth on the list. The restaurant features traditional Chinese-inspired interiors accented by modern paintings and floral arrangements. Floor-to-ceiling windows offer panoramic views of the city. Its menu blends classic Cantonese cuisine with contemporary touches and Southern Asian influences. Signature dishes include Peking duck and dim sum. Bassac Restaurant at Victoria Chau Doc Hotel in Vietnam's Mekong Delta province of An Giang ranks ninth. For lunch and dinner, the restaurant offers a diverse menu of Western and Asian dishes alongside regional Vietnamese specialties. The menu caters to both international travelers seeking familiar flavors and local diners looking to sample well-prepared regional cuisine. Local favorites such as fish noodle soup, sizzling pan bread, noodles, beef steak and pho are also served there. Address: 1 Le Loi, Chau Quoi 3 Area, Chau Doc Ward, An Giang Lava Restaurant at InterContinental Phu Quoc Long Beach Resort in An Giang's Phu Quoc Island finished the top 10. It serves up flavor-rich grilled dishes featuring hand-picked fresh seafood and premium imported beef. Distinguished by its bamboo-vaulted ceiling and striking fossilized coral bar, the restaurant offers a range of dining spaces, from an airy outdoor terrace to intimate private rooms suited to private gatherings. The Travelers' Choice Awards Best of the Best title is awarded to those who receive a high volume of above-and-beyond reviews and opinions from the Tripadvisor community. picked.t: 221 passengers evacuate Air Seoul flight to Vietnam after fire breaks out in bag, power bank suspected
picked.body: Smoke began rising from a bag a passenger had stowed under a seat on flight RS511 at around 9 p.m. local time and soon turned into a fire, according to Air Seoul. The bag held a power bank kept in a pouch, Korea JoongAng Daily reported. Crew members put out the flames using bottled water and other means before firefighters arrived to check on passengers, The Chosun Ilbo reported. Some passengers complained of breathing discomfort, but none needed hospital treatment and no injuries were reported. The aircraft had 228 people on board, including seven crew members. Many of the passengers were families heading to the central Vietnamese city for Chuseok, South Korea's autumn harvest holiday. Air Seoul had everyone leave the plane and brought in another aircraft so the original could undergo safety checks. The replacement flight took off about two hours and 50 minutes late with 219 passengers, after two chose not to travel. Air Seoul and fire authorities are still working to determine the cause. The passenger had taken measures to prevent the battery from short-circuiting, Korea JoongAng Daily reported. Some passengers have suggested the fire started while the power bank was being used to charge an e-cigarette. Air Seoul said it presumes the power bank caught fire but is "still verifying the facts, including whether it was in use," The Chosun Ilbo reported. Since April 20, South Korea has limited air passengers to two power banks each and banned using or recharging them on board, under rules it drafted and the International Civil Aviation Organization adopted as a global standard. Passengers must keep the batteries with them, sealed in a bag or insulated, and not in overhead bins, Korea JoongAng Daily reported. The rules followed a January 2025 fire that destroyed an Air Busan jet at Gimhae International Airport in Busan after a power bank stored in an overhead bin ignited.

picked.t: Indian man dies after motorbike collides with van on Da Lat pass
picked.body: At around 6 p.m. Friday, the two men were traveling by motorbike from Da Lat toward southern Dong Nai Province via the pass. Near the Datanla Waterfall in Xuan Huong Ward, their vehicle collided with a van traveling in the opposite direction. The crash killed a 26-year-old man at the scene. His 24-year-old companion suffered multiple injuries and was rushed to Lam Dong General Hospital for emergency treatment. Authorities have not yet determined which of the men was driving the motorbike. At the scene, the motorbike was found in the opposite lane surrounded by scattered debris, while the van had stopped in its lane a short distance away. The road was wet from recent rain. The injured man was transferred to a hospital in Ho Chi Minh City early on Saturday at his family's request. Authorities are investigating the cause of the crash. The 7.27-kilometer Prenn Pass is a major gateway connecting National Highway 20 with downtown Da Lat. The winding road, which runs through hills and pine forests, was widened to four lanes in early 2024.

picked.t: Hanoi's oldest hotel: A century of change, with guests from Charlie Chaplin to Donald Trump
picked.body: The Grand Hôtel Métropole Palace was built on the site of what was once a lake. Archival photo When it first opened, it was the largest hotel in Indochina, described by Revue Indo-Chinoise magazine as "huge." Its facade stretched more than 80 meters. A view of the hotel's exterior in 1908. The hotel was co-founded by Gustave Émile Dumoutier, an education official, and André Ducamp, a French investor, under the name Société Française Immobilière, a French real estate company. During the first half of the 20th century, it was a meeting place for Hanoi's upper class. In 1920, when Hanoi had yet to have a cinema, a foreign silent film was screened at the Metropole's Hotel Grand Café for guests. The screening was among the earliest film shows in the city, with silent films typically being accompanied by live music. During the struggle against French colonial rule, the hotel became a venue for receiving politicians, diplomats and internationally renowned figures. In 1936, comedian Charlie Chaplin and his wife stayed at the hotel for their honeymoon after a secret wedding in Shanghai. In the early 1940s (photo), the French owner sold the hotel to a Chinese businessman. After peace was restored in 1954, the Métropole was renamed Thong Nhat Hotel and placed under the management of the Hanoi People's Committee, and became a venue for receiving guests of the Vietnamese government. During his first visit to Hanoi circa 1954, writer Graham Greene stayed at the Métropole and recorded his experiences in his novel "The Quiet American." From 1969 to 1981, Thong Nhat Hotel served as the headquarters and residence of several embassies and embassy staff. Most embassy buildings in Hanoi had to be rebuilt at the time, and so the hotel became a residence for diplomatic representatives. The photo shows the Heritage Wing, the historic building that retains the hotel's French colonial character, viewed from Con Coc flower garden and from the rear on Ly Thai To Street, around the 1970s. At the time, the hotel also operated under the Sofitel name and was among the top-end properties in the Legend group. Some 10 years later, the office floors were converted for hotel use. In 1996, the hotel joined a global group of renowned hotels. That same year, it was recognized by the Vietnam National Authority of Tourism as Hanoi's first five-star hotel. picked.t: From cassava-stretched meals to Hanoi pastry kitchen: Hmong baker supports family of 10
picked.body: One morning in August, the auditorium at KOTO’s vocational training center in Bac Ninh fell silent as May, 26, stepped onto the stage. No longer the shy teenager who arrived 7 years ago, she spoke confidently about her journey from a childhood of sparse meals in the mountains to a pastry kitchen at an upscale restaurant in the capital. May is the eldest of eight children in a family of 10 in Pu Xi Village, Muong Mun Commune, Dien Bien Province. Her childhood meals often consisted of rice mixed with grated cassava. During the lean season before the harvest, the family sometimes had only rice soaked in plain water and eaten with ginger preserved in salt. May recalled that her mother, who was often in poor health, had never been able to go to the hospital. She rose early and worked late, chopping duckweed and sweet potato leaves to feed the pigs and chickens before heading to the family’s upland fields. May said she began carrying her younger siblings on her back around the house and village when she was 3 or 4. As she grew older, she would carry a younger sibling to the district market. In blazing midday heat or steady rain, she trudged 5 to 6 kilometers along muddy mountain roads with a small child on her back, helping her mother sell goods. "I don’t remember what we sold, but I clearly remember what it felt like to carry one of my siblings on my back," May said. May said watching mothers and older sisters spend their lives in the village, making sacrifices for their families, convinced her that she had to study hard and build a different future. Near the end of high school, May learned about a free two-year vocational program run by KOTO, a social enterprise that supports disadvantaged young people. Her family could not afford university tuition, so the program covered vocational training and conversational English classes leading to an internationally recognized certificate. When May was accepted, her mother, Sung Thi Sai, 46, gave her just enough money for a bus ticket. "Study hard and be a good person, so you won’t have to suffer as much as we have," her mother said. May joined KOTO’s K35 cohort in July 2019. At first, modern kitchen equipment intimidated her, and she was afraid to speak up or communicate in English. She said the welcoming environment, where trainees were not treated differently because of where they came from, gradually helped her gain confidence. Although the COVID-19 pandemic disrupted her studies, May received an Outstanding Trainee certificate and placed third in a baking competition organized by the center. She also completed an internship at a five-star hotel in Hanoi and joined a field trip to central Vietnam. "I realized how vast the world beyond my hometown was—and that I could be part of it, too," she said. After graduating, May began making pastries at a restaurant in Hanoi’s West Lake area. She started sending money home as soon as she received her first paycheck. Whenever her parents fell ill or her siblings needed tuition money, May contributed as much as two-thirds of her income. She said her support meant her mother no longer had to gather wild vegetables to sell. May said her example had encouraged her younger siblings. Those still living in their hometown have set their sights on becoming an auto mechanic, a teacher and a filmmaker. May hopes to open her own bakery. For now, however, helping support her family remains her highest priority, even if it means postponing that goal. "Living 500 kilometers from home can be lonely, but I always remind myself that I have to keep moving forward," she said.
